chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, who said:

I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: He was asked about what is permissible and what is not permissible regarding the intention by concealment (in the heart) in an oath. He said: It is permissible in one case and not permissible in another. As for what is permissible: when one is the oppressed party, whatever he swears with and intends for the oath is upon his intention. And as for when he is the oppressor, the oath is upon the intention of the oppressed party.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on intention in oaths when one is oppressed versus when one is the oppressor?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of 'niyyah' in oaths by distinguishing between the oppressed and the oppressor, establishing that the oath's validity aligns with the party's actual intent. Specifically, if the swearer is the oppressed, the oath follows their own intention; if they are the oppressor, it follows the intention of the oppressed party. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on fairness and the protection of the weaker party's intent in legal declarations.
